title: The Yellow House
subtitle: Hope, Crisis and the Work of Recovery
introduction: In Arles, Vincent hoped to build a place where artists could live and work together. Gauguin’s arrival brought that possibility into the rooms of the Yellow House.

Their weeks together brought shared subjects, experiments with observation and memory, and uncertainty about the household’s future. On 23 December 1888, Vincent experienced a severe crisis and injured himself.
Follow the story through their correspondence, the reports of others, and the work Vincent made as he tried to resume his life.
contentNote: This story discusses self-injury and mental distress. No graphic imagery is shown.

entry.title: A Room for Gauguin
entry.paragraph: Vincent prepared the Yellow House for a life shared with another painter. Two sunflower paintings hung in the room intended for Paul Gauguin. The invitation carried his hope that artists could live and work together in the south.

chapters.label: A Place for Two
chapters.title: Gauguin Arrives
paragraphs: Gauguin arrived in Arles on 23 October 1888. Vincent had prepared the Yellow House and its sunflower paintings for a companion with whom he could live and work.
The invitation belonged to a larger hope: a community of artists in the south. In the next chapter, enter the daily arrangements and artistic experiments that made this first partnership real.

chapters.label: Working Side by Side
chapters.title: Two Artists in One House
paragraphs: Two painters now shared the Yellow House. Their partnership involved the work of keeping a home, making pictures and talking through what art could become.
Follow four parts of that shared life: a household becoming a studio, experiments with memory, a portrait of a companion, and the town beyond their door.

readings.label: A Shared Working Life
readings.title: A Household Becoming a Studio
paragraphs: Theo was part of this household even from Paris. His financial support and his work as an art dealer helped sustain Vincent and his arrangement with Gauguin. Vincent’s letters connect the sale and sending of paintings with the costs of living and working.

In early November, Vincent listed a chest of drawers, household utensils and twenty metres of canvas bought by Gauguin. They recorded the expenses for later repayment. Gauguin also had plans of his own, including another journey to Martinique.

Their working days took them to the Alyscamps, an avenue of tombs and tall poplars. Both made paintings there. Compare how the path recedes, how trees divide the surface, and how small the figures become. Neither canvas is simply a copy of what the eye sees.

people.name: Vincent
people.role: A home and a studio community
people.text: Invited Gauguin, prepared the rooms and hoped shared work could develop into a community of artists.

people.name: Paul Gauguin
people.role: A partner with plans of his own
people.text: Worked with Vincent, contributed household purchases and continued to consider his own artistic and travel plans.

people.name: Theo
people.text: Supported Vincent, sold work by Gauguin and remained involved through money, paintings and letters.

readings.label: Observation, Memory and Imagination
readings.title: How Does Experience Become a Painting?
paragraphs: Before Gauguin arrived, Vincent explained to Émile Bernard that an actual model or subject gave his work direction. Starting from life did not mean reproducing appearances mechanically: he could change colour, simplify forms and intensify expression.

Gauguin encouraged him to compose through memory and imagination. This was not a contest between a realist and an inventor. Both selected and transformed experience, and Vincent tried another way of bringing it into a picture.

Painted in Arles, Memory of the Garden at Etten brings an earlier place into a new scene. In a letter to Willemien, Vincent connected its figures and colours with their mother and Wil without claiming literal likenesses. Choose a detail below to follow his explanation.

observations.label: People
observations.text: The two foreground women can call their mother and Wil to mind without being their exact portraits. Vincent asks his sister to read associations in the figures rather than identify a literal family scene.

observations.label: Colour
observations.text: Dark violet clothing, an orange-and-green scarf and the emphatic garden colours help carry character and feeling. In his explanation, colour does more than describe the local appearance of things.

observations.label: Memory
observations.text: The painting was made in Arles, not in the Etten garden before his eyes. Earlier experience is reorganised in a new composition. Vincent links this experiment to conversations with Gauguin.

readings.label: Painting One Another
readings.title: Gauguin’s Image of Vincent
paragraphs: Gauguin painted Vincent seated at work on sunflowers, joining his companion to a subject already associated with him.

Museum research places the portrait in December, when Vincent was not painting fresh sunflowers. Memory and reference to earlier paintings shape this scene: it is Gauguin’s image of Vincent at work, not a transparent record of a sitting.

Look at the concentrated figure, the flowers and the act of painting. Gauguin’s later account of Vincent’s reaction is discussed in Sources & Versions, rather than staged here as a witnessed conversation.

readings.label: The Town After Dark
readings.title: Cafés, Brothels and Possible Subjects
readings.date: 1 or 2 November 1888 · An earlier café painting from September
paragraphs: Their shared life extended beyond the studio. In the joint letter to Émile Bernard of 1 or 2 November, Vincent reported going to brothels with Gauguin and discussed what might be painted there.
The letter supports a shared activity and a search for subjects. It does not establish how often either man went, every purpose or encounter, or a causal link with the later crisis.

The Night Café was painted in September 1888, before Gauguin’s arrival. It offers an earlier view of a café in Arles, not a brothel interior and not evidence of the two painters making this picture together.

chapters.label: Staying or Leaving
chapters.title: The Future of the Household
paragraphs: By December, the continuation of their shared life had become uncertain. Around 11 December, Vincent thought Gauguin had become discouraged by Arles, the Yellow House and Vincent himself. He hoped the partnership could continue.

The prospect then shifted. Vincent’s letter of 17 or 18 December describes their museum visit and intense discussions of Delacroix and Rembrandt. The accompanying letter from Gauguin to Theo, identified by the editors, drew back from his earlier plan to leave for Paris.

On 22 December, Gauguin told Émile Schuffenecker he was staying for now, though departure remained possible. This statement survives in his correspondence, cited in note 28 to Letter 726; it is not a decision reported in Vincent’s own words.

The sequence contains concern, renewed conversation and a provisional decision to remain. It should not be flattened into an inevitable march towards disaster. The next chapter follows the crisis of 23 December; artistic disagreement alone cannot establish its immediate cause.

readings.label: Around 11 December
readings.title: The possibility of leaving
paragraphs: Vincent considers Gauguin’s discouragement and the possibility of his departure. This is Vincent’s view of an uncertain situation, not a record of a final decision or a witnessed quarrel.

readings.label: 17 or 18 December
readings.title: Artistic conversation continues
paragraphs: Vincent describes the visit to Montpellier and discussions of Delacroix and Rembrandt as “excessively electric”. Note 28 identifies an accompanying letter in which Gauguin withdrew his plan to return to Paris. Keep Vincent’s description and Gauguin’s decision in their separate voices.

readings.label: 22 December · Gauguin’s Decision
readings.title: Staying, without closing the possibility of leaving
readings.badge: GAUGUIN’S CORRESPONDENCE · CITED IN EDITORIAL NOTE 28
paragraphs: Writing to Schuffenecker, Gauguin said that he was staying in Arles for now, while leaving remained possible. The scholarly edition cites this correspondence in note 28 to Letter 726. It preserves a provisional choice, not a promise that the household could continue indefinitely.

chapters.label: 23 December
chapters.title: A Crisis in Arles
paragraphs: On the evening of 23 December, Vincent experienced an acute crisis and cut his left ear with a razor.
A local newspaper later reported that he went to a brothel and handed the severed ear to a woman it called Rachel. Police found him at home the following morning, and he was taken to hospital.
The surviving accounts leave gaps in the sequence of events. Gauguin’s description of their encounter comes through his own accounts and the reports of others.

chapters.label: A Woman Called Rachel
chapters.title: The Woman Behind the Report
chapters.date: 23 December 1888 · A later visit on 2 February 1889
paragraphs: The report names her Rachel. Vincent brought the severed ear to a woman at a brothel in Arles; beyond this moment, her own life has often disappeared from the story.

Bernadette Murphy’s later research identifies her as Gabrielle Berlatier, a farmer’s daughter who had survived a dog bite and treatment earlier that year. Martin Bailey subsequently published her surname. Murphy describes her as a maid, rather than a sex worker. These are attributed research findings, not facts established by the newspaper alone.

Read the event, the identity research and the proposed motives separately, then return to Vincent’s account of a later visit. None establishes a romantic relationship or a certain reason for choosing her.
chapters.readingsLabel: THE EVENT · THE PERSON · THE INTERPRETATION

readings.label: The Report
readings.title: A Name in the Newspaper
paragraphs: The newspaper’s local-news item describes an event on the previous Sunday, 23 December. At about 11.30 in the evening, it reports, Vincent arrived at brothel No. 1, asked for Rachel and gave her his ear, with the words ‘Keep this object carefully’. Those words belong to the report: they are not independently recovered dialogue.

According to the same account, police found him at home the following morning and took him to hospital. The scholarly letter edition reproduces and compares the report with other accounts. This panel is a summary, not a facsimile or an invented eyewitness scene.

The Van Gogh Museum’s account likewise describes self-injury and a visit to a brothel; it calls the recipient a prostitute. Murphy’s later research offers a different account of her occupation. An institutional summary, a contemporary report and later research should not be mistaken for the same kind of evidence.

readings.label: Tracing Gabrielle
readings.title: A Life Before That Night
readings.date: Medical history in 1888 · Research published in 2016
paragraphs: Murphy traced a young woman named Gabrielle but withheld her surname. Following clues in her book and medical records at the Institut Pasteur, Bailey identified her as Gabrielle Berlatier, a farmer’s daughter living near Arles.

Bailey reports that a rabid dog bit her left arm on 8 January 1888. Local cauterisation came before anti-rabies treatment in Paris. She was eighteen at treatment and nineteen by December. The injury left a scar; the journey and associated expenses placed pressure on her family.

Murphy describes work as a maid and cleaner at the brothel. The registration age for sex workers was twenty-one, but Bailey cautions that the rule was not always observed. Age alone therefore cannot settle her occupation.

Murphy also suggests she may have worked at the Café de la Gare, where Vincent lodged. That possible connection does not prove they already knew each other. The underlying medical documents are discussed through these researchers’ accounts; no reconstructed archive page is presented here.

readings.label: Why Her?
readings.title: Compassion, a Scar and an Unanswered Question
paragraphs: Murphy proposes that Gabrielle’s scar might have mattered to Vincent. In her interpretation, during the crisis he may have imagined offering his own healthy flesh to repair another person’s injury. She connects this possibility with compassion and religious ideas of sacrifice.

This is Murphy’s proposed explanation, not a documented statement of Vincent’s intention or a demonstrated medical diagnosis. His surviving words do not say that he meant to heal her scar. The possible café connection is not proof of the motive either.
The question remains open. This interpretation should not turn a distressing act of self-injury into a romantic gesture, a successful treatment or an established act of rescue.

readings.label: A Later Visit
readings.title: Returning to See Her
readings.date: Letter 745 · 3 February 1889 · Describing a visit on 2 February
paragraphs: On 3 February, Vincent told Theo that he had gone back the previous day to see the woman he had approached during the crisis. He wrote that she had suffered, had fainted and had since regained her composure. He also described her sympathetically, as someone of whom people spoke well.

The letter is a first-person record of a later visit, not a full account of the December night. It does not give her name or explain why he brought her the ear. It brings her distress back into view without confirming Murphy’s later identification or proposed motive.

chapters.label: Care and Concern
chapters.title: News from the Hospital
paragraphs: Gauguin sent a telegram to Theo on 24 December. Theo took the night train to Arles to see his brother in hospital. Gauguin left Arles in the days following the crisis.
Doctors and friends kept Theo informed. On 30 December, Félix Rey described an improvement in Vincent’s condition while acknowledging how difficult it was to answer Theo’s questions with certainty.
Rey also wrote about his own experience of being far from his family. His letter brings a personal voice into the record of Vincent’s care.

people.name: Theo van Gogh
people.text: Travelled to Arles and remained central to the correspondence about Vincent’s care.

people.name: Félix Rey
people.text: Reported improvement while acknowledging the limits of what he could know.

people.name: Joseph Roulin
people.text: Wrote to the family and accompanied Vincent after he left hospital.

readings.label: From the Doctor
readings.title: Félix Rey to Theo
paragraphs: Rey reports that Vincent’s condition has improved, but cannot offer certainty about what will follow. He also recalls his own separation from his family. Clinical observation and personal sympathy both have a place in this letter.

readings.label: From a Friend
readings.title: Joseph Roulin to Willemien
paragraphs: Roulin writes about Vincent’s return from hospital and his own efforts to accompany him. The letter presents recovery through the practical actions of a friend. Roulin accidentally wrote the year as 1888; the scholarly edition dates it to 1889.

chapters.label: Returning to Work
chapters.title: A Face in the Studio
paragraphs: Vincent returned home on 7 January. He told Theo that he intended to begin with still lifes to regain the habit of painting. He also planned a portrait of Félix Rey.
That month, he painted Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear. A canvas on an easel and a Japanese print appear behind him. The bandage records the injury within an image of himself as a working painter.

On 17 January, he reported that he had begun working again. The same letter counted hospital payments, laundry and other expenses. Recovery involved finding strength, paying bills and returning to his materials.

hotspots.label: The Bandage
hotspots.text: The injury was to Vincent’s left ear. Working from a mirror reversed his features: the bandage is on the figure’s right, which is the viewer’s left. This is a self-portrait in a studio, not an image of the injury itself.

hotspots.label: The Canvas
hotspots.text: A canvas on an easel stands behind him. Its presence brings the setting back to work: a room with the materials and possibilities of painting, not only a place of suffering.

hotspots.label: The Japanese Print
hotspots.text: The Japanese print on the wall recalls his sustained interest in Japanese art. Together with the easel, it places the injured man within the visual world of a working artist.

readings.label: 7 January · Returning Home
readings.title: Regaining the habit of painting
paragraphs: Home again, Vincent proposes starting with still lifes and making a portrait of Rey. These are plans for specific pieces of work, not evidence that his recovery is complete.

readings.label: 17 January · Work and Bills
readings.title: The practical life of recovery
paragraphs: Vincent reports returning to work while accounting for hospital costs, laundry and other expenses. Read these ordinary obligations beside the self-portrait: a life is being resumed through materials, money and care.

chapters.label: Living in Arles
chapters.title: Illness, Neighbours and Confinement
paragraphs: Further crises interrupted Vincent’s recovery. In February, a petition signed by thirty residents asked the authorities to have him committed.

The petition and police report recorded fears and allegations about his behaviour. Vincent’s letter of 19 March gives another view: he described being confined, distressed by the accusations and unable to use his studio.
Read together, these records reveal a difficult relationship between illness, public concern and personal freedom. Each document speaks from a particular position.

readings.label: The Petition
readings.title: A document of public concern
readings.date: February 1889 · Thirty signatures on the surviving petition
paragraphs: The petition records the residents’ fears and allegations. Their statements must remain attributed to the document, rather than being retold as established acts. The scholarly annotations link the petition and police material.

readings.label: Vincent’s Response
readings.title: Confinement and the inaccessible studio
paragraphs: Vincent describes confinement, distress over the accusations and his inability to use his studio. He says that more than eighty people signed, whereas the surviving petition bears thirty signatures. His experience and the surviving document should both be visible; neither number should silently replace the other.

chapters.label: Seeking a Place of Care
chapters.title: The Decision to Go to Saint-Rémy
paragraphs: In a letter to Willemien written between late April and early May, Vincent described repeated crises and his plan to enter an institution at Saint-Rémy.
He continued to think about the course of his work, the books he was reading and the life he hoped to regain.
On 8 May 1889, he entered Saint-Paul-de-Mausole. The admission documents record his wish for care and observation. His next year of painting would take shape within this new setting.

readings.label: Read About the Decision
readings.title: Seeking a setting for care and work
readings.date: Letter 764 · Between about 28 April and 2 May 1889
paragraphs: The letter to Willemien describes repeated crises and the proposed move. The admission register records his entry on 8 May. These are separate documents: the decision and the institutional record should not be presented as the same moment.

evidence.title: Gauguin’s Account
evidence.subtitle: A Recollection Written Later
paragraphs: In Avant et après, written in 1903, Gauguin described Vincent approaching him with an open razor. A letter from Émile Bernard to Albert Aurier dated 1 January 1889, reporting what Gauguin had told him, gives a different account of the encounter.
These texts reach us through different moments and narrators. They require comparison; neither is a recording of the evening.

evidence.title: The Extent of the Injury
evidence.subtitle: A Drawing by Félix Rey
paragraphs: Accounts differed over how much of the ear was removed. In 1930, Félix Rey drew the injury for the writer Irving Stone. Preserved at the Bancroft Library, the note and drawings support an injury involving almost the entire external ear.
The drawing was made decades after Rey treated Vincent. It is not an 1888 hospital chart.
evidence.contentNote: The external source includes a medical drawing of the injury. It is not displayed in this gallery.
evidence.linkLabel: View the Medical Drawing at Berkeley

evidence.title: The Woman in the Report
evidence.subtitle: Rachel and a Later Identification
paragraphs: The contemporary report uses Rachel. Murphy’s 2016 identification and Bailey’s subsequent archival work propose Gabrielle Berlatier and describe a young maid. Bailey also cautions against using the registration age alone to prove her occupation.
Letter 745 records a later visit but does not name her. Identity, occupation, acquaintance and motive are separate questions; establishing one would not automatically establish the others.

evidence.title: The Museum’s Account
evidence.subtitle: A present-day synthesis, not an eyewitness report
paragraphs: The Van Gogh Museum describes Vincent injuring himself on 23 December, wrapping the ear and taking it to a woman in a brothel. Its page calls her a prostitute. It does not establish a scar-healing motive.

This museum narrative supplies the exhibition’s basic sequence of crisis, care and renewed work. Its wording about the recipient should be compared with Murphy’s later occupation research, not silently combined with it.

evidence.title: An Explanation Is Not an Intention
evidence.subtitle: Murphy’s reading of the scar and sacrifice
paragraphs: Murphy suggests that Gabrielle’s injury and religious ideas of sacrifice might help explain the gift. The argument is hers: no surviving statement by Vincent identifies healing her scar as his purpose.

The chapter offers this interpretation for examination, not as an official conclusion or a retrospective diagnosis. Letter 745 records concern and a later visit; it cannot verify that proposed motive.

evidence.title: An Alternative Reconstruction
evidence.subtitle: The Gauguin Hypothesis
paragraphs: In their 2008 book, Hans Kaufmann and Rita Wildegans proposed that Gauguin injured Vincent with a sabre and that the artists concealed what had happened.

This is a later reconstruction advanced by those authors. It differs from the Van Gogh Museum’s account of self-injury. The presence of several narratives does not give them the same evidential weight.

evidence.title: The Portrait and a Later Reaction
evidence.subtitle: Gauguin’s retrospective voice
evidence.badge: LATER RECOLLECTION · NOT A WITNESSED DIALOGUE
paragraphs: The museum catalogue discusses Gauguin’s later claim that Vincent recognised himself in the sunflower portrait but thought he looked like a madman. This reaction reaches us through Gauguin’s retrospective account, not a contemporary transcript of Vincent speaking.
Read it as evidence of how Gauguin later told the story. It should not be turned into invented speech or used to diagnose Vincent from the painting.
